questions.stem: A 34-year-old man developed pustular, suppurative, nodular lesions over his arms that increased in size and quantity over 3 months. He had severe myasthenia gravis and had been taking prednisone 40 mg per day for 18 months. The lesions were unresponsive to a 14-day course of doxycycline and a subsequent 14-day course of oral trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole. On examination:
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Ascending lymphangitis secondary to Nocardia spp. infection

questions.explanation: Nodular granulomatous perifolliculitis (Majocchi’s granuloma) Nodular granulomatous perifolliculitis (Majocchi’s granuloma) occurs when dermatophytes invade hair follicles leading to granulomas and/or suppuration. The same organisms which are responsible for tinea corporis and/or pedis (Trichophyton rubrum, T. mentagrophytes, Epidermophyton floccosum, etc.) are involved. Occlusion, trauma to skin (e.g., shaving), use of topical steroids on unsuspected tinea, and immunocompromised states increase risk. It presents as subacute to chronic nodular lesions that progressively increase in size and number after dermatophyte invasion of hair follicles. Look for cluster(s) of pustules/ papules/nodules within erythematous scaling plaques, that may resemble bacterial furuncles or carbuncles. Treatment requires systemic antifungals.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q49

questions.stem: A 42-year-old man presented with a 1-week history of fever and productive cough. He had a deceased donor renal transplant 7 months ago. He was taking tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and prednisone. On exam his temperature was 38.6°C Investigations: CXR: left lower lobe nodule with central cavitation Sputum microscopy revealed long, crooked, branching, beaded gram-positive filaments
questions.lead_in: What would be the most appropriate empiric therapy?
questions.explanation: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and imipenem The patient is immunocompromised due to his transplantation and presents with a cavitary lung lesion. He is at risk for many opportunistic pathogens but has Gram stain findings suggestive of infection due to Nocardia. Two-drug therapy with sulfamethoxazole and imipenem would be recommended empirically and the patient will likely require a minimum of 6 months of treatment.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q8

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man presented with a 6-week history of a left buttock mass. It was nontender, and he was otherwise asymptomatic. He thought it may be related to a minor trauma when he scraped himself on a yucca plant while gardening. He had received an allogeneic stem cell transplant 9 months earlier for acute myelogenous leukemia, which had been complicated by graft versus host disease of the skin and gastrointestinal tract. He was taking prednisone 20 mg od, tacrolimus, inhaled pentamidine, and aciclovir. On examination, his temperature was 37°C, his blood pressure was 145/73 mmHg, heart rate 88 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and oxygen saturations 99% on room air. He was overweight, in no acute distress, and he had a grapefruit-sized mass on his left buttock. The rest of the exam was unremarkable. Investigations: Total white cell count 8.6 ×109/L Hemoglobin 12.5 g/dL Platelets 146 ×109 /L eGFR >60 mL/min per 1.73 m2 Aspiration of the mass revealed gram-positive branching filamentous rods.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Nocardia farcinica Nocardia farcinica is an opportunistic pathogen found in soil and water, which can cause skin and soft tissue infections when it gets into open wounds or cuts. The typical appearance on Gram stain is as gram-positive branching filamentous rods. Treatment of choice is trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole. Mycobacterium abscessus is a nontuberculous mycobacterium which would appear as acid-fast bacilli on acid-fast staining. It can cause nodular and ulcerative lesions in areas of trauma. Stenotrophomonas maltophilia is a multidrug-resistant gram-negative pathogen that can cause ventilator-associated pneumonia. Scedosporium prolificans is an opportunistic fungus that can cause infections in immunocompromised patients and would not appear as a gram-positive filamentous rod. Listeria monocytogenes would appear as a gram-positive rod on Gram stain, not filamentous, and causes meningitis in immunocompromised patients.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q26

questions.question: A 3 year-old previously healthy girl presents with red, tender, and swollen inguinal lymph nodes that started 4 days ago. She has a small ulcer ipsilateral to the lymph nodes. Her parents say she sustained minor trauma here approximately 3 days before the lymph nodes developed. An aspirate is performed. 3 days later, culture is positive for a branching and beaded gram positive bacilli

parts.text: What is the most likely organism (to genus level)?
List THREE medications that should be could in initial treatment.

questions.model_answer:
a) Most likely organism (genus level): Nocardia (lymphocutaneous nocardiosis from traumatic skin inoculation, mimicking sporotrichoid spread).
b) 3 medications to consider for initial treatment: (1) trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, (2) minocycline, (3) amoxicillin-clavulanate (linezolid is an additional accepted alternative).

questions.question: Patient with cavitary lung disease and GPB on gram stain

parts.text: What are 4 GPB that are partially acid fast?
The colonies on agar are salmon pink, which is the most likely organism to the genus level?

questions.model_answer:
a) 4 partially acid-fast gram-positive bacilli: Nocardia, Rhodococcus, Tsukamurella, and Gordonia.
b) Salmon-pink colonies on agar - most likely genus: Rhodococcus (Rhodococcus equi classically produces salmon-pink/coral-colored mucoid colonies).

questions.question: Picture of nodular lymphangitis of the arm. They take a sample for microbiologic testing. They give you four images of stains and you have to identify the organism in each stain that would cause these lesions (something like these pictures)

parts.text: [image-based question: Gram stain - gram positive cocci (could not agree whether clusters or chains)]
[image-based question: Gram Stain - Branching gram positive bacilli]
[image-based question: H&E stain]
[image-based question: Grocott Gomori Methenamine Silver Stain - Yeast]

questions.model_answer:
a) Gram stain showing gram-positive cocci (in clusters or chains): suggests a bacterial cause of nodular lymphangitis such as Staphylococcus aureus (clusters) or Streptococcus pyogenes (chains).
b) Gram stain showing branching, beaded gram-positive bacilli: Nocardia brasiliensis (also weakly acid-fast/modified acid-fast positive).
c) H&E stain: cigar-shaped budding yeast forms consistent with Sporothrix schenckii (though organisms are often sparse and difficult to visualize on H&E).
d) GMS (Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver) stain showing yeast: Sporothrix schenckii (cigar-shaped budding yeast highlighted well by GMS when H&E is unrevealing).
questions.beyond_mandell: Without the actual images, the gram stain organism identifications (a, b) are inferred from the classic sporotrichoid/nodular lymphangitis differential rather than directly confirmed.

questions.question: Q8 (2006 PM). 35 year old male with Hodgkin's disease with lung nodules and ring-enhancing lesions in the brain.

parts.text: a) What is the most likely bacterial cause?
b) How would you investigate (not including blood cultures)?
c) How would you treat this patient if he is allergic to penicillin?

cohort_answer.text: a) Nocardia. DDx for lung/brain axis: bacterial (Rhodococcus equi, Anaerobes, S. anginosus, S. aureus, K. pneumoniae hypermucoviscous, Mycobacteria, Actinomyces), fungal (Aspergillus, Mucormycosis, Crypto neoformans). b) BAL; MRI brain (preferred in all suspected pulmonary/disseminated nocardiosis); lung nodule biopsy for cultures/pathology (nocardia culture, fungal culture, AFB, C/S); brain biopsy/aspirate for cultures/pathology; serum CrAg; BAL galactomannan. c) TMP-SMX + Imipenem + Amikacin first line for severe CNS disease (TMP-SMX monotherapy for CNS disease associated with >50% mortality); alternatives: linezolid, 3rd gen ceph (ceftriaxone/cefotaxime/cefuroxime) based on susceptibilities. IV therapy minimum 6 weeks then oral (minocycline, amoxicillin/clavulanate, fluoroquinolones, macrolides based on susceptibility). Total duration for CNS infection minimum 12 months.

questions.question: 20-something with recurrent SSTIs and PNA, always Staph aureus. You suspect CGD.

parts.text: what other congenital immunodeficiency could this be?
what is one test for CGD?

Patient stopped taking prophylactic septra. Shown smear with branching GPB. Asked for genus.
[image-based: smear with branching GPB]
What is other prophylaxis should be given to patients with CGD?

cohort_answer.text: Other immunodeficiency: Hyper IgE. Test for CGD: Dihydrorhodamine or nitroblue tetrazolium (oxidative burst). Genus: Nocardia. Other prophylaxis: Itraconazole, Interferon-gamma (proven to reduce severity/frequency of infections)

questions.question: 22. Kid with recurrent skin infections and several episodes of pneumonia requiring hospitalization.

parts.text: What other primary deficiency can look like this
You think this is CGD, what test do you do?
What is the problem with the immune system?
CXR shows LLL lower lobe pneumonia and Kinyoun Acid Fast stain shown, what is the organism?
Treatment
What other prophylaxis do you need in CGD other than TMP-SMX

questions.model_answer:
a) Other primary immunodeficiency that can mimic this picture: Hyper-IgE (Job) syndrome (STAT3 deficiency).
b) Test for CGD: dihydrorhodamine (DHR) flow cytometry assay (measures neutrophil oxidative/respiratory burst); NBT test is an older alternative.
c) Immune defect: mutation in components of the NADPH oxidase complex (most commonly X-linked gp91phox) causing failure of the neutrophil respiratory burst and defective killing of catalase-positive organisms.
d) Kinyoun (modified acid-fast) stain of an LLL pneumonia in CGD: organism is Nocardia species (partially acid-fast, branching filamentous gram-positive rods).
e) Treatment: TMP-SMX (high-dose) or, for sulfa allergy/severe disease, linezolid or a carbapenem plus amikacin, guided by susceptibilities and often combined with surgical drainage.
f) Additional CGD prophylaxis beyond TMP-SMX: itraconazole (antifungal, especially anti-Aspergillus) prophylaxis, and interferon-gamma.

questions.question: A 51 year-old man, on dexamethasone for a glioblastoma, is admitted with fever and progressively worsening respiratory symptoms x 18 days. CT chest shows multiple non-cavitary nodules measuring 1.5 to 5 cm. Placed on piperacillin/tazobactam and ciprofloxacin, but continues to worsen despite this treatment. After 4 days, respiratory cultures grow dry, yellow colonies. Beaded, filamentous Gram-positive rods are seen on Gram stain.

parts.text: a) What is the pathogen?
b) What is the most important next test?
c) What are three other Gram-positive rods that can grow aerobically that can cause a similar clinical picture?

cohort_answer.text:
a) What is the pathogen? - Nocardia spp
b) What is the most important next test? - Modified Acid fast staining - main DDx = Actinomyces which does not stain with modified acid fast but nocardia does (CT head if you already have identified the pathogen) [source note: Uptodate]
c) What are three other Gram-positive rods that can grow aerobically that can cause a similar clinical picture? - Rhodococcus, Gordonia, Tsukumeullea, Streptomyces - also GPB but not pathogenic so wouldn't include in this answer but FYI
cohort_answer.source: AB 2019 (answer slides (with Gram stain and Acid-Fast Staining images interspersed); speaker notes citing Uptodate for part b)

parts.text: Guy with vasculitis on steroids who has ring enhancing lesions in brain and lung nodules. List 3 possible organisms and first line empiric treatment regimen

cohort_answer.text: Possible organisms: Nocardia, Staph aureus, Streptococcus anginosus. Empiric treatment: Ceftriaxone, vanco, metro (empiric bacterial coverage); Septra, imipenem +/- amikacin (Nocardia); TB - RIPE + steroids if meningitis; Cryptococcus - amphoB + flucytosine, then fluconazole

questions.question: [image-based question: picture of sporotrichoid spread with 4 different stains shown, asked to identify the organism for each]

parts.text: Stain 1 (Leischmania)
Stain of nocardia branching GPCs in chains
A gram stain with 30% GPC, rest looked either washed out or like GNC either solo or in short chains, clusters as well (Francisella tularensis)
Sporothrix stain, ~2microns in size (given legend up to 20 microns, nothing over 2-3 microns in size)

cohort_answer.text: Stain 1: Leishmania. Stain 2: Nocardia (branching GPCs in chains). Stain 3: Francisella tularensis (gram stain with ~30% GPC, rest washed out/GNC solo or in short chains/clusters). Stain 4: Sporothrix (~2 microns in size).

questions.question: Q93 2023 Day 2. Name 4 partially acid-fast organisms. Then shown agar plate with mucoid/salmon colored colonies growing and asked to identify. (MICRO)

parts.text: Name 4 partially acid-fast organisms
[image-based: identify the organism forming mucoid/salmon colored colonies on the agar plate shown]

cohort_answer.text:
4 partially acid-fast organisms: Nocardia spp; Rhodococcus; Gordonia; Tsukamurella (all partially acid-fast, aerobic, Actinomycetes, branching filamentous bacteria that fragment into rods and cocci).
Mucoid/salmon colonies: Rhodococcus spp - non-hemolytic, round, often mucoid with orange to red/salmon-pink pigment within 4-7 days. (For comparison: Nocardia colonies highly variable, some beta-hemolytic, wrinkly, dry, chalky-white to orange-tan, crumbly; Gordonia colonies smooth, mucoid, adherent, beige/orange/yellow/pink/white to gray; Tsukamurella colonies rhizoid edges, white or creamy to orange.)

questions.question:
Q17 (2011 PM) Brain + Lung lesions
AML patient presenting with dyspnea and R sided weakness. Cavitary lung lesions and one brain lesion
Alternate wording: SLE patient on cyclophosphamide and prednisone. Develops lung nodules and brain abscess. List 3 organisms and their tx?
List 3 organisms and initial empiric tx?

parts.text: List 3 organisms and initial empiric tx?

cohort_answer.text: Nocardia: TMP/SMX + imipenem/meropenem + amikacin. Aspergillus: Voriconazole. Tuberculosis: INH/RIF/ETH/PYZ + steroids. Cryptococcus neoformans: Amphotericin B + Flucytosine (treatment phase) → Fluconazole (consolidation and suppressive phases). Actinomyces (A. meyeri, odontolyticus, israelii): Penicillin + surgery for CNS. Streptococcus anginosus: Ceftriaxone. S. aureus: Vancomycin.

questions.question: Q7 (2010 PM). Scenario with immunocompromised patient who develops pulmonary symptoms, found to have lung nodules. Started empirically on PipTazo and Vanco, continues to be febrile and lung nodules are worsening. Sample taken, and gram stain shows filamentous GPB.

parts.text: A) Most likely diagnosis
B) Single most important test at this point
C) Two other aerobic gram positive rods that can cause a similar picture

cohort_answer.text: A) Pulmonary nocardiosis. B) AFB stain - modified acid-fast staining (Kinyoun stain or auramine-rhodamine fluorescent stain) can make presumptive diagnosis; Nocardia differentiated from Actinomyces by acid-fastness and aerobic growth. C) Rhodococcus equi, Gordonia.
